content: If hypersensitivity reactions occur during the use of thiabendazole, the drug must be discontinued immediately and should not be resumed. Erythema multiforme has been associated with thiabendazole therapy, and in severe cases, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, fatalities have been reported. Central nervous system (CNS) side effects are relatively common with this medication; therefore, activities requiring mental alertness should be avoided. Cases of jaundice, cholestasis, and parenchymal liver damage have been reported in patients treated with thiabendazole (MINTAZOL). In rare instances, liver damage has been severe and has resulted in irreversible hepatic failure. Adverse effects involving the eyes, such as abnormal sensations, xanthopsia, blurred vision, drying of mucous membranes, and Sicca syndrome, have been reported in patients treated with MINTAZOL. In some cases, these ocular side effects have persisted for prolonged periods, exceeding one year. Thiabendazole is not typically recommended as a first-line therapy for the treatment of enterobiasis. It should be reserved for patients who have experienced allergic reactions or resistance to other treatments. MINTAZOL is not suitable for treating mixed infections involving Ascaris, as it may cause these worms to migrate. Supportive therapy is recommended for anemic, dehydrated, or malnourished patients before initiating anthelmintic treatment. Patients with hepatic or renal dysfunction should be carefully monitored during treatment. MINTAZOL should only be used in patients with a confirmed diagnosis of susceptible worm infestation and should not be used prophylactically. Patients should be informed that CNS side effects are relatively common, and they should avoid activities requiring mental alertness while on this medication. In rare cases, a transient rise in liver function test results has been observed in patients receiving MINTAZOL. Thiabendazole has been extensively studied in animals at doses up to 15 times the usual human dose and has not demonstrated carcinogenic effects. It has not adversely affected fertility in mice at doses 2.5 times the usual human dose or in rats at doses equivalent to the human dose. Additionally, thiabendazole has shown no mutagenic activity in in vitro microbial mutagen tests, the micronucleus test, or the host-mediated assay in vivo. Reproductive and teratogenic studies in rabbits, rats, and mice at doses up to 15 times the usual human dose have shown no evidence of harm to the fetus. However, in one study in mice, cleft palate and axial skeletal defects were observed when thiabendazole was suspended in olive oil and administered at 10 times the usual human dose. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. MINTAZOL should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. It is unknown whether thiabendazole is excreted in human milk. Due to the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, a decision should be made to either discontinue nursing or discontinue the drug, considering the importance of the drug to the mother. The safety and effectiveness of thiabendazole for treating strongyloidiasis, ascariasis, uncinariasis, trichuriasis, and trichinosis in pediatric patients weighing less than 30 lbs have not been well established. Clinical studies of MINTAZOL have not included sufficient numbers of subjects aged 65 and older to determine whether they respond differently from younger patients. However, other reported clinical experiences have not identified differences in responses between elderly and younger patients. In general, dose selection for elderly patients should be cautious, starting at the lower end of the dosing range, reflecting the greater frequency of decreased hepatic, renal, or cardiac function, and the presence of concomitant diseases or other drug therapies. Thiabendazole is almost completely metabolized by the liver, and its metabolites are substantially excreted by the kidneys. Therefore, the risk of toxicity may be higher in patients with impaired renal function. Since elderly patients are more likely to have decreased renal function, care should be taken in dose selection, and monitoring of renal function may be useful.
